analysis.one_liner: Rebuilt deposit insurance to protect small savers while letting bank companies expand into securities, insurance, and nationwide banking.
analysis.headline: This sweeping 1991 banking bill never got a House vote of its own; its depositor-protection core became law as part of the FDIC Improvement Act, while its bank-power expansion did not.
analysis.plain_summary: After the savings-and-loan bailout, this bill rewrote deposit insurance so taxpayers' fund would cover ordinary savers instead of large investors who spread money across banks to multiply coverage. It also forced shaky banks to pay higher insurance premiums, restricted risky activities, and required banks to tell customers that mutual funds sold in branches are not FDIC-insured. At the same time, it would have let companies own banks, securities firms, and insurers together — repealing key Glass-Steagall separation rules — and allowed nationwide branching over state objections. The bill never got a floor vote; it was folded into H.R. 6, which became the FDIC Improvement Act of 1991 with the safety reforms but without the expansion.
analysis.who_benefits: Small savers and pension holders, whose insurance protection gets a clear $100,000 cap per institution and stops subsidizing large investors who used brokers to spread deposits across banks for extra coverage. Taxpayers gain from least-cost bank resolutions, risk-based premiums charged to risky banks, and 'prompt corrective action' that forces regulators to fix weak banks before they fail. Bank customers gain one-stop financial services, nationwide branches, and required disclosures that investment and insurance products sold by bank affiliates are not FDIC-insured.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small savers, taxpayers, and bank customers

how_it_helps.text: Caps deposit insurance at $100,000 per depositor per institution and excludes brokered deposits and pension-plan investment contracts from insurance, closing the loopholes that let large investors multiply coverage at the deposit insurance fund's expense.
Bars banks that fall below minimum capital from luring deposits with interest rates far above prevailing rates — the classic pattern of a failing institution gambling for rescue with insured money.

Requires the FDIC to resolve bank failures at the least cost to the insurance fund, sets up 'prompt corrective action' with escalating restrictions for undercapitalized banks, and directs risk-based insurance premiums so safer banks pay less and riskier banks pay more.

Requires prominent written disclosure — acknowledged by the customer — that securities and insurance products sold by bank affiliates are not deposits, are not FDIC-insured, and are not guaranteed by the bank.
Permits financial services holding companies, nationwide branching, and a wider range of financial products, which the bill's stated purposes frame as consumer convenience and competition.

analysis.who_pays: Banks pay risk-based insurance premiums, new capital and examination requirements, and restrictions on state-chartered banks' activities; credit unions owe new capitalization payments and premiums to their insurance fund. Deposit brokers lose their main business of placing insured deposits for large investors. Securities and insurance firms face competition from bank conglomerates entering their markets. States lose the power to block out-of-state acquisitions and branching.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large banks, deposit brokers, securities and insurance firms

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the Glass-Steagall bans on bank affiliation with securities firms and on shared personnel, letting single companies combine banking, securities underwriting and dealing, and insurance — creating large conglomerates whose deposit-taking arm is federally insured.
It authorizes nationwide banking and preempts state laws that block affiliations, acquisitions, and interstate branching, stripping states of a major tool for limiting bank concentration.

It preserves a too-big-to-fail back door: the Federal Reserve and Treasury may jointly direct the FDIC to provide assistance beyond least-cost when a failure would severely harm the financial system — the kind of exception that protected large uninsured depositors during the 1980s.

It raises the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act exemption threshold from $10 million to $50 million in assets, cutting public reporting on home lending by smaller institutions and limiting fair-housing data collection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The deposit-insurance overhaul — a hard $100,000 cap, no insurance for brokered deposits, risk-based premiums, least-cost resolutions, and prompt corrective action — was a genuine, well-targeted fix for the taxpayer losses of the S&L era, and Congress enacted that core. The financial-services expansion was the costly part: it would have concentrated banking, securities, and insurance in the same companies, preempted state law, and kept a systemic-risk exception for protecting big depositors, and Congress declined to enact it at the time. On balance, the bill's consumer-protection half was sound; its industry-expansion half carried serious concentration and conflict-of-interest risks that the eventual law avoided for years.

outcome.mechanism: After months of hearings and a subcommittee rewrite, the bill was folded into H.R. 6 — the FDIC Improvement Act of 1991 — and never received a floor vote of its own.

narrative.text: Introduced March 20, 1991 by Rep. Henry Gonzalez, the House Banking Committee chairman, 'by request' — the House convention for a bill requested by the executive branch — and referred to three committees the same day.

The Financial Institutions Subcommittee held repeated hearings in spring and summer 1991 and marked the bill up in four sessions in May, forwarding an amended version to the full committee on May 23, 1991; more hearings followed through September.
The full committee never completed action; the last entry in the bill's action history, dated November 4, 1991, reads 'For Further Action See H.R. 6.'

H.R. 6 became the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Improvement Act of 1991, enacted that December, which adopted the prompt corrective action, least-cost resolution, and risk-based premium framework — but not the financial-services holding company, Glass-Steagall repeal, or nationwide branching provisions of H.R. 1505.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Small depositors and taxpayers came out ahead: the bill's deposit-insurance safeguards became law through H.R. 6, while the provisions expanding bank powers into securities and insurance were left out. Large banking companies had to wait — eventually gaining nationwide branching in 1994 and affiliations with securities firms in 1999 under later laws.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Small depositors and taxpayers; bank expansion delayed

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan — the Democratic committee chairman joined by the committee's ranking Republican — and it originated as a request from the Republican Bush administration, so the dividing lines ran less by party than over how far to let banks expand.

industries.note: Title II would have handed these companies securities underwriting, insurance, and nationwide branching — powers they later won in 1994 and 1999 — while Title I made them pay risk-based premiums, face prompt corrective action, and accept restrictions on state-chartered affiliates. The reform half protected the insurance fund that backs ordinary savers; the expansion half would have concentrated financial power.

The bill excludes broker-placed deposits from insurance coverage. Brokers earned fees by spreading large deposits across banks so big investors could multiply $100,000 coverage — a practice that shifted risk onto the fund that protects small savers.

The bill opens securities underwriting and dealing to financial holding companies, adding well-capitalized competitors — while also restricting banks themselves to intrastate brokerage and pushing securities activity into separately disclosed affiliates. It also gives the SEC new authority over bank-affiliated mutual funds and requires prominent disclosure that such funds are not FDIC-insured.

Financial holding companies could own insurance affiliates, bringing banks into insurance sales, but insurers could likewise diversify into banking; state insurance agencies lose some preemptive authority over affiliations.

Nationwide banking and branching, plus the preemption of state anti-affiliation laws, would expose local banks to direct competition from large out-of-state institutions, though the same bill tightens supervision of their riskier rivals.

Credit unions would owe new initial capitalization payments, a 1 percent capitalization adjustment, and annual premiums to the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund — costs to the institutions that shore up the fund protecting their members' savings.
